Telling people what I do is usually awkward. Chinese people ask, “Which sheng?” (the Chinese word for acoustics, shengxue, is easy to mishear) or “So you study singing?” Foreigners ask, “So you make speakers? Do you play music?”

Acoustics is interdisciplinary and covers an enormous range: mechanical vibration, aerospace and marine engineering, the automotive industry, architecture and urban planning, music, speech, medicine. Yet it’s also a niche, and not many people work in it.

Historically, acoustics is a branch of physics. Counting from its founding father, Helmholtz, it has been developing for a mere 150 years or so. From the early to the mid-20th century, driven by a group of American and German acousticians such as Sabine, Eyring and Schroeder, architectural acoustics, and room acoustics in particular, flourished, and acoustics was applied mainly to the design of auditoriums, concert halls and the like. Later the applications gradually widened: all kinds of sound-absorbing materials were used across many fields to reduce noise, and for a long time noise reduction was the main goal of the field. Once noise had come down to the point where it couldn’t go much lower, or where people could no longer perceive the change, some pointed out that the ear, the most finely crafted microphone array there is, together with the brain, the smartest processor in the universe, perceives far more than just how loud a sound is. So psychoacoustics was born. Its landmark text, Zwicker and Hugo’s Psychoacoustics, is still the bible of the field. Psychoacoustics puts human perception at the center, and with it came sound quality, a new standard for judging sounds rather than sound pressure level and decibels alone. If human perception is to replace numbers, then sounds should be experienced and judged through more senses than just sight. So in the 1990s the concept of auralization was proposed (the audible counterpart of visualization): a technology that turns sound from cold numbers and signals into a form people can listen to directly. The classic textbook is Auralization by Professor Vorländer in Germany (who was also my PhD supervisor), once again the bible of its field. Auralization covers source modeling, sound propagation modeling and sound reproduction. These drove the development of numerical/computational acoustics and geometrical acoustics, bywords for accuracy and for efficiency respectively, as well as binaural technology and spatial/3D reproduction. Since the audience for reproduced sound is human, medical acoustics developed alongside: cochlear implants, hearing aids, training blind people to sense their surroundings from echoes, and so on. Further toward medicine, there is ultrasound.

Beyond that, there’s underwater sonar, seismic monitoring, radar antenna technology, soundscape (a concept proposed and developed by Professor Jian Kang at UCL), automotive NVH, consumer products such as microphones, loudspeakers and headphones, business products such as data acquisition systems, sound cards and Microflown’s sensors, and the speech and language recognition that’s so hot right now. You name it.

In short, it depends on which direction you go. Acoustics covers so much ground that mastering all of it is next to impossible.

PS: After writing all this, I really feel like writing a history of acoustics XD

More on acoustics (popular science, curiosities, little-known facts, industrial applications, case studies and where the field is heading) on my WeChat Official Account, Ziyu Acoustics.
